intuition: Carry a depth beside each node you visit. The root has depth 1, and each child has its parent's depth plus 1. Save the largest depth seen. This measures the longest root-to-leaf path without needing to list every complete path.

A recursive solution can return one plus the larger child depth, but a highly skewed tree may exceed Python’s recursion limit. An explicit stack stores pairs of node and depth instead. Start the root at depth one, and give every pushed child its parent’s depth plus one.

The maximum over all visited node depths equals the maximum leaf depth because an internal node with a child cannot be the end of a longest path. There is no need to store complete paths or to separately recognize leaves. An empty root produces an empty stack and leaves the answer at zero.
The stack retains only unfinished branches rather than every visited node.

steps: The tree [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] has root 3. Start stack=[(3,1)] and best=0.
Pop root 3 at depth 1 and set best=1. Push children 9 and 20 with depth 2.
Pop node 20. best becomes 2; push its children 15 and 7 with depth 3.
Popping either child establishes best=3. The remaining child at depth 3 and node 9 at depth 2 cannot increase it.
Once the stack is empty, every node has been considered. Return 3.

codeNotes.note: The initial depth counts the root itself. An absent root naturally creates no work and yields depth zero.
Every stored depth is exact, so maintaining its maximum is sufficient without copying paths or checking leaf status.
Adding a child extends its root path by exactly one node; recording the depth alongside the node preserves that invariant.

keyDecision: Depth counts nodes here. An empty tree has depth 0.

concept.question: How does counting nodes along each root path reveal the deepest leaf?
intuition: Listing complete root-to-leaf paths stores more than the answer needs. A node’s depth can be carried during a visit without retaining its entire path.
Give the root depth one. Each child has one greater depth than its parent. Visit all nodes and remember the greatest depth encountered.
concept.observation: Depth counts nodes from the root, so an existing root starts at one.
approach: Visit a node with its depth.
Visit children with one greater depth.
concept.correctness: A node’s assigned depth equals its parent’s correct depth plus one, starting from the root’s one. Thus every assigned depth is its actual root-path node count. Visiting all nodes includes a deepest leaf, and taking the greatest assigned depth yields the tree’s maximum depth.

complexity.explanation: Visit each node once. An iterative depth-first frontier holds pending paths proportional to tree height in the worst case.

pitfalls: Depth counts nodes from the root, so an existing root starts at one.
Do not count only edges when the requested depth counts nodes.
